title: Hammock localization as a colimit of fixed-type hammock graphs
statement:
Use the small signed-word category $\mathcal I$ and proper simplicial-set diagrams defined in [lem-coef-proper-word-colimit-invariance], and write $\mathbb H=\mathcal I$. Encode a word $h$ of length $l$ as $(S,T_0)$, where $S$ is its set of $+$ positions and $T_0$ its set of $-$ positions. Use the ordinary fixed-word diagram categories and their nerves from [def-coef-zigzag-homotopy-calculus]. Let $P$ be a small ordinary category, $T\subseteq P$ a wide subcategory (containing every object and identity and closed under composition), and $x,y\in P$. For $h=(S,T_0)\in\mathbb H$ of length $l$ define $G_{P,T}(h)(x,y)_q$ to be the commutative hammocks in $P$ with $q+1$ rows, $l$ columns and endpoints $x,y$ in every row. Vertical arrows point down and lie in $T$, and endpoint vertical arrows are identities. Column $i$ points right if $i\in S$, and left with arrows in $T$ if $i\in T_0$. Identity columns and adjacent columns of the same direction are allowed. Faces delete rows and compose intervening vertical arrows, and degeneracies repeat rows. A morphism $f:h'\to h$ sends such a diagram of type $h'$ to type $h$ by composing the columns in each fiber $f^{-1}(i)$ and inserting an identity column when the fiber is empty. This defines a proper functor $G_{P,T}(-)(x,y):\mathbb H\to\mathrm{sSet}$. Let $H(P,T)(x,y)$ consist of the same diagrams reduced by deleting entirely identity columns and composing adjacent columns with the same direction; the reduced diagrams have alternating column directions and no entirely identity column. Include the length-zero diagram precisely when $x=y$, and define faces and degeneracies by row deletion/repetition followed by reduction. Reduction gives a natural isomorphism
$$\operatorname{colim}_{h\in\mathbb H}G_{P,T}(h)(x,y)\cong H(P,T)(x,y).$$
Both the diagram and this isomorphism are natural for functors of pairs preserving the wide subcategories, including their simplicial operators when $P,T$ vary simplicially on a fixed object set.

source.place: Dwyer–Kan, Calculating simplicial localizations, Definition 5.1 and Propositions 5.4–5.5, printed p.24, with Definitions 2.1, 4.1 and 5.3. Our word positions follow the horizontal columns from left to right (the displayed source word is written in composition order). No Stacks tag states this result.

proof.text: For each signed word $h$, take the category $Z_h(x,y)$ of [def-coef-zigzag-homotopy-calculus], using only its $+$ and $-$ letters, and set $G(h)=NZ_h(x,y)$. A string of $q$ morphisms is exactly the stated $q+1$-row hammock: its successive vertical maps lie in $T$, and its endpoint maps are identities. For a morphism $f:h'\to h$ of [lem-coef-proper-word-colimit-invariance], every nonempty fiber is a consecutive block with the sign of its image position. Number source and target vertices starting at zero. At target vertex $i$ retain source vertex $k_i=|\{j:f(j)\leq i\}|$ and its vertical arrows; in particular $k_0=0$ and $k_l=l\prime$, where $l\prime$ is the source length. The columns in the fiber at $i$ connect source vertices $k_{i-1}$ and $k_i$. Compose that block, in its arrow direction, and insert an identity at that vertex for an empty fiber. Commutativity of the original squares makes the resulting squares commute; closure of $T$ under composition handles negative blocks and composed vertical maps. If two word maps are composed, the two procedures compose exactly the same ordered blocks, with identities for missing positions, so associativity and units give $G(gf)=G(g)G(f)$ and $G(1)=1$. The same identities show that these operations commute with all nerve row operators. Thus $G$ is the asserted functor to simplicial sets.

source.place: Definitions 4.1 and 5.1–5.3, printed pp.22–24; explicit verification of the fixed-word construction

proof.text: An injective word map inserts entirely identity columns and leaves all retained horizontal arrows unchanged. Conversely a hammock of the target shape lies in its image exactly when every omitted column is entirely identity. Indeed, in any identity column the objects on its two sides agree in each row, and its commuting squares force their vertical arrows to agree, so deleting these columns recovers a unique source hammock, including its vertical arrows. This proves degreewise injectivity. Given two injections into the same word, belonging to both images means that the columns outside either image are identities, equivalently that every column outside their intersection is identity. The preceding deletion construction gives precisely the image of the intersection injection. This is both clauses of properness in [lem-coef-proper-word-colimit-invariance]. If the intersection is empty, deletion forces every row to be the same endpoint $x=y$ and all vertical maps to be endpoint identities; otherwise the intersection image is empty, as required.

source.place: Definition 4.4 and Proposition 5.4, printed pp.23–24; identity-column image calculation

proof.text: Fix a row degree. Use the two elementary reductions of [lem-coef-hammock-reduction-diamond]. Each reduces the column count by one, so successively reducing while a move is available ends in at most the original number of columns. Apply [lem-coef-rewrite-common-reduct] to this relation on the small set of all unreduced hammocks of this degree and these endpoints. Its fork hypothesis follows from [lem-coef-hammock-reduction-diamond]: equal outputs have themselves as common reduct, and unequal outputs have the stated one-step common reduct; one step is in particular a finite sequence. Consequently any two finite reduction sequences from $D$ have a common further reduct. If both outputs are terminal, neither can take a step, so that common reduct equals both outputs. This proves existence and uniqueness of the terminal reduct $R(D)$. By the two move definitions, terminal means alternating directions and no entirely identity column. Length zero exists exactly for equal endpoints and is the constant identity hammock. Finally, by the word-map definition of [lem-coef-proper-word-colimit-invariance], composing a same-sign pair is a surjective word-map relation, while deleting an identity column reverses an injective word-map relation. Thus every $D$ represents the same colimit class as $R(D)$.

source.place: Definition 2.1 and Proposition 5.5, printed pp.19,24; termination by column count, strong diamond input, and the existing general common-reduct lemma

proof.text: Every word map factors into the surjection onto its ordered signed image and the injection of that image into the target word: list the occupied target positions in increasing order. A surjection composes consecutive equal-sign blocks and is a sequence of pair compositions; an injection inserts identity columns. Hence every word-map relation preserves $R$, by step 3, including its reverse. Conversely two diagrams with the same $R$ are connected by their respective finite reductions to that same diagram. By the degreewise quotient-colimit assertion of [lem-coef-proper-word-colimit-invariance], the map $[D]\mapsto R(D)$ is therefore well-defined, injective and surjective in each row degree; the inverse sends a reduced diagram to its colimit class. To check simplicial structure, let $\alpha$ be a raw nerve row operator of [def-coef-zigzag-homotopy-calculus]. It sends an identity deletion to an identity deletion and a same-sign composition to that same composition, since restriction to rows and vertical composition preserve the horizontal composites and their squares. Thus applying $\alpha$ to any reduction sequence gives a sequence of valid reductions, and uniqueness gives $R(\alpha R(D))=R(\alpha D)$. Define the row action on reduced diagrams by $R\alpha$. Then $R\alpha R\beta=R\alpha\beta$, so the raw nerve identities give all simplicial identities after reduction. The degreewise bijections commute with these operators and constitute the required simplicial-set isomorphism.

source.place: Definitions 2.1, 5.1, 5.3 and Proposition 5.5, printed pp.19,24; quotient identification and row-operator check

proof.text: Let $F:(P,T)\to(P',T')$ be any functor of pairs. Applied entrywise to unreduced hammocks, it preserves endpoint identities, distinguished arrows, commuting squares and ordered composites. It therefore commutes with each fixed-word structure map and with each raw row operator. It sends each reduction move to a valid reduction move, so uniqueness gives $R(F(R(D)))=R(F(D))$. Define its action on reduced hammocks by $D\mapsto R(F(D))$; the displayed equality proves compatibility with reduction and with composition of pair functors, even when $F$ sends further nonidentity arrows to identities or identifies endpoints. On the colimit class of every representative $D$, both sides of the naturality square are $R(F(D))$, so the reduction isomorphism is natural. When pairs vary simplicially on a fixed object set, apply this argument to each simplicial structure functor: for a structure functor $F$ and a raw row operator $\alpha$, the equality just proved gives $R F R\alpha=R F\alpha=R\alpha F=R\alpha R F$. Thus the two reduced directions commute. Identities and composites of the structure functors satisfy their simplicial identities after reduction because $R F R=R F$. Hence the assertion also respects every simplicial operator in that parameter.
